codeB.answer:
**Short answer:** Don't stop paying rent over this. Florida's rent-withholding protection covers only the repairs the statute lists, and your lease, not the statute, promises the air conditioning. You may be able to end your lease, but you haven't started that process yet. Your portal request doesn't start it, because it didn't say you would end the lease. To start it, you would deliver a separate written notice by hand or by certified mail, then give the landlord 7 days to fix the AC. Whether a two-week AC outage is serious enough to count is not settled, so I can't promise it would work.

What would change this is what the office has told you about when the part will arrive. If the delay is outside the landlord's control and the landlord keeps working on it, a different rule applies (see the last heading below).

DETAILS

### Can you stop paying rent until the AC is fixed?
- Florida lets a tenant raise a defense for unpaid rent only for a "material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)" (83.60(1)(b)). Section 83.51(1) covers codes, structural parts, and plumbing. It does not name air conditioning.
- Your AC is covered by your lease, which says the landlord "will keep them in working order: refrigerator, stove, dishwasher, and central air conditioning" (Lease §11). That makes it a lease promise, not a listed 83.51(1) duty. The rent-withholding defense doesn't reach it.
- A local building or housing code might also cover cooling. The codes aren't stored in this tool, so the city or county code office can tell you.
- Withholding rent also risks an eviction case. You haven't sent a notice saying you will not pay rent, and that notice is a requirement even for the repairs the statute does cover.
- Your June rent was paid before the AC failed. July rent is due July 1.

### Can you end the lease?
Section 83.56(1) lets a tenant end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof." Here is how your facts fit each part:
- **A promise the landlord failed to keep:** Lease §11 promises working central air conditioning, and it has been out since June 3.
- **Whether that is "material":** This is not settled, because the statute doesn't define the word. One reading is that any failure of a lease promise counts. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it lasts, and how it affects living there. Under that second reading, 90 degrees inside for about two weeks supports you, but a court decides.
- **Written notice:** You haven't sent this yet. Your June 4 portal request asked for a repair but did not say you would end the lease, so it is not this notice. Section 83.56(4) names the ways to deliver it: mailing it or delivering a true copy. The portal is not one of those ways, and a lease can't waive these rules. Your lease says notices go "by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail" (Lease §7). Your lease has no e-mail agreement (Lease §8).
- **The notice must say two things:** what is wrong, and that you intend to end the lease because of it.
- **7 days:** The 7 days run from the day the notice reaches the landlord, not the day you send it. I can count them once you have a delivery date.
- **Rent paid:** Paying rent while you know about a problem can give up your right to end the lease over it (83.56(5)(a)). You paid June rent before the AC failed, so that hasn't happened. If you pay July rent while the AC is still broken, it is not settled whether that gives up your right. One reading is that an unfixed problem is a "continuing noncompliance," so nothing is given up. The other is that paying with knowledge gives up the right for that failure.

If you do end the lease and move out, the deposit rules apply.

### What else can you do?
- **Damages:** Section 83.55 says the "aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." It covers lease promises like this one and requires no notice. The winner of a suit may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.
- **Code complaint:** A complaint to the code office is allowed. The law protects you from retaliation for a good-faith complaint (83.64(1)(a)).

### Does the "part on order" change anything?
When the landlord can't comply for reasons beyond its control and keeps making every reasonable effort, 83.56(1) says the lease "may be terminated or altered by the parties." If the home becomes untenantable and the tenant moves out, no rent is owed for that period (83.56(1)(a)). If the tenant stays, rent is reduced in proportion to the loss (83.56(1)(b)). Whether the part delay is beyond the landlord's control is open, and so is what "untenantable" means. It is also not settled whether "terminated or altered by the parties" requires both sides to agree.

Has the office told you when the part is due, or said anything else about the repair besides "a part is on order"?

To end the lease, you first have to send a written notice that says you will end it, and your portal request wasn't that notice. Delivering that notice starts a 7-day clock. DETAILS

### Is the AC your landlord's job to fix?
Yes, under your lease. Section 11 says the landlord "will keep them in working order," and the list includes "central air conditioning." Florida's repair statute (83.51) does not list air conditioning. So your right comes from the lease, unless a Gainesville or Alachua County housing code also requires AC. I can't check local codes. The city or county code office can tell you, and it can inspect.

You told me nothing you know of caused the breakdown. The landlord is not responsible only for damage that you, your family, or your guests caused (83.51(4)). Nothing you've described falls under that.

### Can you stop paying rent?
Not safely. The rent-withholding defense (83.60(1)(b)) covers only "a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)." That section lists codes, structure, and plumbing. An AC that only the lease promises is outside it, unless a local code also covers AC. If you withhold rent and your landlord files for eviction, you probably couldn't use this defense.

Even if a code did cover AC, you would need a written notice that you won't pay rent because of the problem. Then 7 days would have to pass (83.60(1)(b)). Your portal request didn't say that.

If you are ever sued for eviction, you must pay the rent into the court registry, or file a motion about the amount, within the deadline in the summons. If you miss it, you give up your defenses (83.60(2)).

### Can you end your lease?
Not yet. The rule (83.56(1)) lets a tenant end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice." The notice must name the problem and say you intend to end the lease. Here is how your facts fit each part:

- **A lease promise that was broken:** Yes. Section 11 promises working AC.
- **"Material" failure:** This is not settled, because the statute doesn't define the word. One reading is that any broken lease promise counts. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there. Twelve days of 90-degree heat helps you under the second reading.
- **A written notice that says you will end the lease:** Not met. Your June 4 portal request asked for a repair and didn't mention ending the lease. A portal message is also not one of the delivery methods the statute names, which are mailing, delivering a copy, or e-mail under 83.505 (83.56(4)). Your lease says you did not agree to e-mail notices (§8). Lease §7 says notices to the landlord go "by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or "by certified mail" to that address. Either one meets the statute.
- **7 days after delivery:** The clock hasn't started. It runs from the day the notice reaches the office, not the day you send it. I can count the days once you have a delivery date.
- **No rent paid with knowledge of the problem:** Met so far. You paid June rent on June 1, before the AC failed. If you pay July rent while the AC is still broken, it is not settled whether that gives up your right to end the lease over this problem. One reading is that an unfixed problem is a "continuing noncompliance," so paying gives up nothing. The other is that paying rent with knowledge gives up the right (83.56(5)(a)).

### Does "the part is on order" change anything?
It might. If the delay is beyond the landlord's control and the landlord keeps making every reasonable effort, a different rule applies (83.56(1)). If the home is "untenantable" (the statute doesn't define the word) and you move out, you owe no rent while it stays that way. If you stay, the rent is reduced in proportion to the loss of rental value. It is not settled whether that rule needs both sides to agree or applies automatically once its facts are met. This is why the arrival date for the part matters.

### What other options do you have?
- **Damages:** You may be able to recover the damages the broken AC caused you (83.55). The winner in a suit may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48).
- **Retaliation:** A landlord may not raise your rent, cut services, or bring an eviction action primarily to retaliate because you made a good-faith complaint to a code office or sent a repair notice under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)). The statute does not protect a tenant who holds back rent, because "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" count as good cause (83.64(3)).

Your lease promises you a reserved covered space, and the landlord has closed the garage with no reopening date. That is a real problem you can act on. Your main options are to ask for money back (damages), put a request in writing, or give a formal written notice that you will end the lease. Holding back rent is not available for this problem. Having paid May rent while the garage was closed may also weaken some of your options.

The next step is a written request to the landlord for a rent reduction or reimbursement, plus a reopening date. Hand it to the office or send it by certified mail, and keep a copy.

DETAILS

### Does your lease promise the parking space?
Yes. Lease §11 says: "Rent includes one reserved space in the covered, gated garage behind the building, space number 12." I found no lease clause that lets the landlord close the garage, limit its use, or reduce rent when it is closed. That makes the space a promise in the lease. The law covers lease promises as well as the repairs it lists by name.

### Can you hold back rent over this?
No. The rent-withholding defense in §83.60(1)(b) covers only a "material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)". That section covers building, housing and health codes, and structural parts and plumbing. A parking space isn't on that list. It is only a lease promise. If you stopped paying, you would risk an eviction case without that defense.

### Can the rent be reduced?
- **No automatic reduction.** Nothing in the statute cuts rent when an amenity closes.
- **Reduction under §83.56(1)(b).** If a problem is "due to causes beyond the landlord's control" and the landlord keeps making "every reasonable effort" to fix it, rent is reduced "in proportion to the loss of rental value." The landlord ordered this repaving, so it is unclear that this applies. I'd need to know what the landlord has said or done about reopening. The statute also says the lease "may be terminated or altered by the parties." It is not settled whether that means both sides must agree, or whether the reduction applies once the facts fit. Either way, asking the landlord in writing is the practical route.

### Can you recover money (damages)?
Yes, this is likely your best route. Section 83.55 says: "If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." It names no notice step. Your losses could include the lost value of the covered space and any street-parking costs. Amounts and court steps are outside this tool. Under §83.48, the winner of a lawsuit may recover attorney fees and court costs, so a suit can cost you money too.

### Can you end the lease?
You can try, but several points are open. Section 83.56(1) allows ending the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement."
- **Written notice.** Your April 15 visit was spoken only, so it doesn't count. The notice must be in writing, name the closed garage, and say you will end the lease because of it. Lease §7 says to hand it to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send it there by certified mail. Section 83.56(4) also allows mailing or delivering a copy. Lease §8 says the parties have not agreed to e-mail notices, so don't rely on e-mail.
- **Seven days.** The landlord then has 7 days after delivery to restore the space. Delivery means the day it reaches the office, not the day you send it.
- **Whether it is "material."** The statute doesn't define the word, and this is not settled. One reading is that any failure to provide a lease promise is material. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects you. Your facts for the second reading: the garage has been closed since April 10, a sign says "closed until further notice," you have no reopening date, and the space is included in your rent.
- **Your May 1 rent payment.** Under §83.56(5)(a), paying rent "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance" gives up the right to end the lease or sue "for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." This is not settled. One reading is that a garage still closed is a continuing noncompliance, so paying rent gave up nothing. The other is that your payment waived ending the lease over the closure, and only a new failure starts over. Paying June rent with the garage still closed raises the same question.

### What about a code complaint or retaliation?
A code office can say whether a local code covers this. The codes are outside this tool. Under §83.64(1), a landlord may not retaliate against you, for example by raising your rent or cutting services, because you made a good-faith complaint or sent a notice. A court decides whether a landlord's act was retaliation.

**Question:** Besides the sign on the gate, has the landlord told you anything about why the garage is closed or when it will reopen, whether by notice, e-mail, or in person?

Each has open questions, and the biggest is that you paid May rent while the garage was closed. Holding back rent is the risky path here. The law's protection for that covers only certain repair duties, and a parking space isn't one of them. Everything you've done so far was in person, so nothing is in writing yet.

One question: apart from your April 15 conversation, has the landlord or office told you anything else about the repaving, such as a notice, email, flyer, or a work schedule?

DETAILS

### Does the lease promise you the garage space?
Yes. Lease §11 says: "Rent includes one reserved space in the covered, gated garage behind the building, space number 12." I found no lease clause that lets the landlord close the garage, even for repairs. Section 10 says the lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." You told me nothing was signed to change it. Whether a short closure for repaving is a breach is open. One reading is that the space is part of what you pay for, so a closure with no end date breaks that promise. The other is that a temporary closure for upkeep is normal and doesn't break it. Since the closure is now over five weeks old with no reopening date, your facts favor the first reading more than a short closure would. Neither reading is settled.

### Can you just pay less rent?
I wouldn't. Under §83.60(1)(b), a tenant can use unpaid rent as a defense only for a problem with the landlord's duties in §83.51(1). Those are building and health codes, structure, and plumbing. A parking space the lease promises is not on that list. Your landlord could treat unpaid rent as nonpayment and start an eviction case. Whether a local code covers the garage is outside what I can check.

### Can you get money back for the closure?
Possibly. Section 83.55 says: "If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." It names no notice step first. Damages are usually the value you lost, such as the cost of other parking. How much, and the court steps, are outside this tool. A suit can also cost the loser the other side's attorney fees and court costs (§83.48).

There is also a separate rule for a failure that is "due to causes beyond the landlord's control" while the landlord keeps making "every reasonable effort" to fix it (§83.56(1)). It lets the rent be "reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value" if you stay (§83.56(1)(b)). Your landlord ordered this repaving, and no one has given you a date. That makes it unclear this rule fits. It is also unsettled whether the rule applies on its own or only if both sides agree.

### Can you end the lease over this?
Possibly, but not yet. Section 83.56(1) lets a tenant end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice." The notice must say what is wrong and that you intend to end the lease because of it. Here is how your facts fit:
- **A lease promise failed:** The garage space is a lease promise (§11).
- **Material:** The statute doesn't define the word. One reading is that any failure of a lease promise is material. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and its effect on you. Over five weeks without a space is a long time, but you still have a place to park on the street.
- **Written notice:** You have none yet. Under §83.56(4) and lease §7, deliver it by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send it by certified mail. Lease §8 says you haven't agreed to email notices, so email wouldn't count. A portal message or text isn't a method the statute names.
- **Seven days:** The seven days start on the day the notice reaches the landlord. No notice has been delivered, so the clock hasn't started.
- **Paying May rent:** Under §83.56(5)(a), paying rent "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance" gives up the right to end the lease or sue "for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." One reading is that a garage still closed is a "continuing noncompliance," so paying didn't give up anything. The other is that paying May rent with knowledge gave up your rights over the closure so far. This is unsettled.

### Does your April 15 visit count as notice?
No. You asked when the garage would reopen. You didn't say you would end the lease, and it wasn't in writing.

### Are you protected if the landlord retaliates?
Section 83.64(1) makes it unlawful for a landlord to raise rent, cut services, or start an eviction "primarily because the landlord is retaliating." That covers a tenant who sends a notice under §83.56(1). You must act in good faith. Whether a landlord is retaliating is for a court to decide.

- **A lease promise broken.** The garage promise is in the lease, and it is not being kept.
- **Whether it is "material."** The statute doesn't define the word, so this is unsettled. One reading says any broken lease promise counts. ### Did the landlord have to send you anything before keeping the deposit?
- Yes. A landlord who wants to keep any of the deposit must send a written notice of the claim, with the reason. The notice must go "by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.49(3)(a)).

- You confirmed you got no notice of a claim by any means. So nothing in writing about keeping any of the deposit has reached you.
- The statute says what happens if the landlord misses the deadline: it "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant" (83.49(3)(a)). "Forfeits" means loses the right.

### Has the 30-day deadline passed?
This is not settled. The statute counts from "the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), and a lease that ends early can be read two ways.
- **Move-out date reading:** The notice you get tells you the claim comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)). Counted from April 15, the 30 days ended May 15. That has passed, so the landlord would have lost the right to claim against the deposit.
- **Lease end date reading:** Section 83.49(3)(a) opens with "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement." That wording treats moving out and the lease ending as two separate things. Your lease runs to July 31, 2026. Counted from that date, the 30 days end August 30. That has not passed, so the landlord could still send a notice.
- The statute also says that when a lease is ended under 83.56, "the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)" (83.56(6)).
- Under either reading, the 15-day return date of April 30 (counted from your move-out) has passed. Missing it forfeits nothing by itself while the 30-day period is still running (83.49(3)(a)).

Yes.

That names moving out and the agreement ending as two separate things. On this reading the 30 days end on 2026-08-30, which has not passed. The landlord could still send a claim.
- **Reading two: the move-out date.** The statute's required notice to tenants says the landlord's notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)). On this reading the 30 days ended on 2026-05-15, which has passed. The landlord would have lost its claim, and you would be owed the full deposit. The landlord could still sue you for damages afterward.

The 15-day deadline to return a deposit when the landlord has no claim (83.49(3)(a)) is 2026-08-15 counted from the lease end date. That date has not passed. Missing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days are still running.

### Was your early exit valid?
The law lets a tenant end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51(1)... within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement" (83.56(1)). The landlord's duty includes keeping "the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Taking your conditions one at a time:
- **A plumbing duty the landlord failed:** A broken toilet and a leaking pipe are plumbing. You say you did nothing to cause it (83.51(4)).
- **Written notice delivered a way the statute allows:** You handed your March 24 letter to the office, which is a permitted delivery (83.56(4)). It named both problems and said you would end the lease.
- **7 days passed:** They ended on 2026-03-31, and you told me nothing was fixed.
- **No rent paid with knowledge of the problem:** You paid March rent on March 1, before the problem began. You haven't paid since (83.56(5)(a)).
- **"Materially" is not settled.** The statute doesn't define the word. One reading is that any failure of a listed plumbing duty is material. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it lasted, and how it affected living there. Your only toilet was broken and a pipe was leaking, from March 20 until you left.

When a lease ends this way, "the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49(3)" (83.56(6)). That means the landlord must still send a claim notice within the deadline.

You haven't paid April rent, and the landlord hasn't asked for it. The landlord could try to claim it, but only through the written notice described above. Whether you would owe it depends on whether your early exit was valid.

If either side sues over the deposit, "the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney" (83.49(3)(c)). The court also hears these cases sooner than most.

**Short answer:** Your rent does not drop automatically. Florida's law has no rule that cuts rent when a promised extra, like your garage space, is closed. You still have options. You can claim money for the lost parking (damages). You may also be able to end the lease with a written notice. You can't lawfully hold back rent over this. Whether paying May rent hurt your position is unsettled. Whether the closure counts as serious enough is also unsettled.

DETAILS

### Is the garage space something the landlord owes you?
Yes, under the lease. Lease §11 says: "Rent includes one reserved space in the covered, gated garage behind the building, space number 12." The lease has no clause letting the landlord close the garage for repaving or other work. The garage is not on the structural or plumbing list in the repair statute (83.51(1)). Whether a local code covers it is outside this tool. So the promise comes from your lease, not from that statute.

### Can you hold back rent?
No. The rent-withholding defense in 83.60(1)(b) reaches only a failure to meet the duties in 83.51(1). A lease-only promise like parking is not one of those duties. If you stopped paying, you could be evicted for non-payment without that defense.

### Can you end the lease?
Possibly. Under 83.56(1), if the landlord "materially fails to comply with … material provisions of the rental agreement" within 7 days after getting your written notice, you may end the lease. Four things must line up:
- **The promise was broken.** The lease promises the space, and the garage has been closed since April 10.
- **"Material" is unsettled.** The statute does not define it. One reading is that any failure of a lease promise counts. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects you. You have lost a reserved covered space for over a month, with no reopening date.
- **You have not sent the notice.** Asking in person on April 15 is not enough. You need a written notice that names the problem and says you will end the lease because of it. It must be delivered a way the statute allows (83.56(4)). Your lease §7 says to hand it to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send it there by certified mail. Lease §8 says you have not agreed to e-mail notices, so e-mail would not count. A portal message or text would not count either.
- **Paying May rent is unsettled.** Under 83.56(5)(a), paying rent "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance" gives up the right to end the lease for that failure, "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." One reading is that a garage still closed is a continuing failure, so you gave up nothing. The other is that paying rent while you knew about the closure gave up the right to end the lease over it.

### Can you get money for the loss?
Possibly. Under 83.55, a party hurt by a failure to follow the lease "may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." Your loss would be the value of the covered space, plus any real costs, such as street-parking fees. Paying rent with knowledge may also affect your right to sue (83.56(5)(a)), with the same two readings as above. The winner in a suit may recover attorney fees and costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.

### Does the landlord get a pass because the closure is temporary?
Maybe in part, but this is not settled. When a failure is due to causes beyond the landlord's control and the landlord keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it, 83.56(1)(b) says that if you stay, the rent for that period "shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value." Here the landlord chose to do the repaving. Whether that is "beyond the landlord's control" is open. The landlord has also given no reopening date. The statute also says the lease may be "terminated or altered by the parties". One reading is that both sides must agree. The other is that the rent reduction applies once the facts are met.

Do you want to stay through July 31, 2026, or are you thinking about leaving?

**Short answer:** You can't cut your rent on your own. Nothing in the lease or the statute lets you take off a set amount for the closed garage. You do have options. You can sue for the money the closure has cost you. You can send a written notice that you will end the lease if the garage stays closed. A court or the landlord could also reduce your rent, but only if the landlord's reason for the closure fits a narrow exception. Don't stop paying rent over this. The law's rent-withholding protection doesn't cover a parking space, so you could be evicted. Has the landlord said anything, in writing or out loud, about why the garage is still closed or when it will reopen?

DETAILS

### Is the garage a promise your landlord must keep?
Yes. Lease §11 says: "Rent includes one reserved space in the covered, gated garage behind the building, space number 12." The lease has no clause that lets the landlord close the garage, limit its use, or offer parking only as a courtesy. A parking space is not on the statute's list of things a landlord must maintain (§83.51(1)), so the duty comes from the lease. The lease is the only source of the parking promise.

### Can you hold back rent?
No. The right to hold back rent and use that as a defense in an eviction case covers only the duties listed in §83.51(1) (§83.60(1)(b)). Parking is not one of them. If you stopped paying, your landlord could file for eviction, and you would have no defense based on the garage.

### Can you end the lease?
Maybe. Under §83.56(1), you can end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement" within 7 days after getting your written notice. The notice must name the problem and say you intend to end the lease because of it. The notice must also be delivered properly:
- **How to deliver it:** Lease §7 requires hand delivery to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or certified mail to that address. Section 83.56(4) also allows delivery by mail or by handing over a true copy.
- **E-mail:** Lease §8 says you have not agreed to e-mail notices, so e-mail won't work.
- **Your April 15 visit:** Asking the office in person didn't count as this notice. It was not in writing, and it did not say you would end the lease.

Two points are open:
- **Is the failure "material"?** The statute doesn't define the word. One reading is that any failure to give you something the lease promises is material. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects your life there. A closure of over a month, with no reopening date and street parking for you, could fit either reading.
- **Did paying May rent give up your right?** Under §83.56(5)(a), paying rent "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance" gives up the right to end the lease or sue over that noncompliance, "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." You paid May rent on May 1 knowing the garage was closed. One reading is that a garage still closed is a continuing problem, so paying gave up nothing. The other is that paying gave up your right over this closure. I'm not leaning either way.

### Can you get money for the closure?
Possibly. Section 83.55 says that when a party fails to follow the rental agreement, the other party "may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." Your out-of-pocket costs for parking elsewhere and the lost value of a covered, gated space could count. The §83.56(5)(a) question above could also affect this claim. In a suit, the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (§83.48). That cuts both ways. How much you could recover, and how to file, are outside what I can help with.

### Does the statute reduce your rent automatically?
No. Section 83.56(1)(b) does reduce rent "in proportion to the loss of rental value," but only when the problem has causes beyond the landlord's control and the landlord keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it. Here the landlord chose the repaving. Whether the landlord is working to reopen the garage is a fact I don't have, which is why I asked my question. Whether that section requires both sides to agree to a reduction is also unsettled. One reading is that the parties must agree. The other is that the reduction applies once its facts are met.

### Are you protected if you complain?
Yes, if you act in good faith. Under §83.64(1), a landlord may not raise your rent, cut services, or threaten or bring an eviction or other civil action primarily to retaliate against you. A written notice under §83.56(1) is one of the protected acts (§83.64(1)(c)). Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court to decide.

You can't hold back rent over the air conditioning, because Florida law doesn't protect a tenant who does that for this kind of problem. You also can't end your lease yet, but you may be able to. To end it, you have to send a separate written notice, and then your landlord gets 7 days to fix the problem. Your portal request doesn't count as that notice, because it asked for a repair and didn't say you would end the lease. If you stop paying rent anyway, your landlord can file for eviction, and the AC problem wouldn't protect you in that case.

Your lease promises working air conditioning, so a broken unit is a lease problem. You haven't paid rent since the AC broke, which helps you. Whether a failure like this is serious enough to justify ending the lease is an open question that a court decides.

What has the office told you about when the part will arrive?

DETAILS

### Can you stop paying rent until it's fixed?
- Florida's rent-withholding defense covers only a failure to meet the repair duties in the statute's first repair subsection (§ 83.60(1)(b), which refers to § 83.51(1)). Those duties are building, housing, and health codes. Where no code applies, they are the structure and plumbing.
- Air conditioning is not named there. Whether a Gainesville or Alachua County code requires it is outside what I can check. The city or county code office can tell you.
- Your lease does promise it. Section 11 says the landlord "will keep them in working order," and the list includes "central air conditioning."
- A lease promise alone doesn't open the rent-withholding defense. Withholding also requires a separate written notice saying you won't pay rent because of the problem, followed by 7 days.
- If you withhold and your landlord sues, you would have to pay the rent into the court's registry (a fund held by the court) or file a motion about the amount within the deadline in the summons (§ 83.60(2)). Missing that deadline waives your defenses other than payment.

### Can you end your lease?
- This is the better route. The statute lets a tenant end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof" (§ 83.56(1)).
- **A duty the landlord failed:** The lease promises working AC (lease § 11). That is a lease provision.
- **Material:** The statute doesn't define the word. One reading is that any failure of a lease promise counts. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there. You have described 90-degree heat and no repair since June 3.
- **The notice:** It must be in writing. It must name the problem and say you will end the lease because of it. It must be delivered by mail or by handing over a true copy (§ 83.56(4)).
  - Your lease § 7 matches this. It says to hand-deliver to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send it there by certified mail.
  - A portal message isn't a delivery method the statute names.
  - Your lease says you have not agreed to e-mail notices (§ 8), so e-mail is out too.
- **Seven days:** The 7 days run from the day the notice reaches your landlord. No notice has been delivered yet, so the clock hasn't started.
- **Rent:** Paying rent while you know about the problem can give up your right to end the lease over it (§ 83.56(5)(a)). You paid June rent before the AC broke, so that isn't a problem. July rent is due July 1.
  - If you pay it while the AC is still broken, it's unsettled whether you keep the right. One reading is that an unfixed problem is a "continuing noncompliance," so paying gives up nothing. The other is that paying with knowledge gives up the right over that failure.
- Moving out without sending the notice would put you at risk of owing rent under the lease.

### Does the landlord's "part on order" change this?
- If the cause is beyond your landlord's control and it keeps making every reasonable effort, a different rule applies (§ 83.56(1)). If the home is unlivable and you leave, you owe no rent for that time. If you stay, rent is reduced in proportion to the loss in value (§ 83.56(1)(a) and (b)).
- Whether that fits here depends on what the office has said and done. The statute doesn't define "untenantable." Whether this rule lets you end the lease alone or needs your landlord's agreement is also unsettled.

### What else can you do?
- **Damages:** You can recover damages caused by a failure to follow the lease (§ 83.55). Rent paid while you know of the problem may affect that right too (§ 83.56(5)(a)). The winner in a suit may recover attorney fees and costs (§ 83.48).
- **Code office:** A complaint to a code office is protected from retaliation (§ 83.64(1)(a)). Retaliation includes raising rent, cutting services, or suing you because you complained. You must act in good faith, and a court decides whether your landlord acted primarily to retaliate.

ruleA.answer:
Yes, the deposit is yours unless your landlord makes a proper, timely claim against it. Your landlord has told you nothing, and it is not settled whether its time to make a claim has run out. If that time has run out, your landlord loses the right to keep any of the $1,050 and must return all of it. It could still sue you for damages afterward. If the time has not run out, your landlord can still send a claim notice by certified mail to the new address you gave it. Either way, you do not have to wait quietly: if either side sues over the deposit, the winner can be awarded court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.

One question: did you return the keys to the office on April 15, or on a different day?

DETAILS

### Is the landlord's 30-day deadline over?
This is not settled, because you left before the lease's end date of July 31, 2026. The statute says a landlord that plans to keep part of a deposit must send written notice "within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). It does not say which date ends the agreement when a tenant leaves early. There are two readings.

- **Move-out date.** The statute's required tenant disclosure says the notice must come "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)). Section 83.56(6) also says that when a tenant ends the lease, "the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)." Thirty days from your move-out date of April 15 was May 15, 2026, and that date has passed. Under this reading the landlord missed its deadline.
- **Lease end date.** Section 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement," which names moving out and the lease ending as two separate things. Thirty days from July 31, 2026 is August 30, 2026, and that date has not passed. Under this reading the landlord could still send a claim notice.

### Did any claim notice reach you?
No. You confirmed that you have received nothing from the landlord, by any means. The only proper notice is one sent "by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address or by e-mail" under a signed e-mail addendum (83.49(3)(a); 83.505(1)). Your lease says the parties "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail" (lease §8). Nothing has been sent, so on this point the landlord has not met the requirement.

### Did you give the notice the law requires for leaving early?
Yes. A tenant who leaves before the lease ends must give "at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery" that includes an address where the tenant can be reached (83.49(5)). You handed a letter to the office on April 2 with your new address. The last day to give it was April 8, 2026, so you were on time. Lease §7 also allows delivery by hand to the office.

### Did you have the right to end the lease?
That matters because it affects whether the landlord can say you owe rent. Section 83.56(1) lets a tenant end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1)" within 7 days after written notice. The notice must name the problem and say the tenant will end the lease.

- **Duty.** Section 83.51(1)(b) requires "the plumbing in reasonable working condition." A broken toilet and a leaking pipe are plumbing problems. Whether a local code also covers them is outside this tool.
- **Cause.** You said you did nothing to cause the problem (83.51(4)).
- **Notice.** Your March 24 letter was handed to the office, which is a delivery method the statute names (83.56(4)). It named both problems and said you would end the lease.
- **Seven days.** The 7 days ended March 31, 2026, and the problems were not fixed.
- **Rent.** You paid March rent on March 1, before the problem started. Paying rent with knowledge of a problem can give up the right to end the lease (83.56(5)(a)), but that does not apply here.
- **"Material."** The statute does not define this word, so that part is not settled. One reading is that any failure of a listed duty counts. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem was, how long it lasted, and how it affected living there. You described your only toilet being out and a leak.

### What about the 15-day return?
If a landlord plans no claim, it must return the deposit "within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). Fifteen days from your move-out date was April 30, 2026, and that date has passed. Missing it does not by itself cost the landlord its claim while the 30-day period is still running.

### Does the lease change any of this?
No. Lease §5 says the deposit is held in a separate account and cannot be used for the last month's rent. Lease §6 asks you to leave the apartment clean, return the keys, and give a forwarding address in writing. You gave the address, and I do not yet know about the keys.

ruleA.answer:
**Short answer:** The law doesn't automatically lower your rent because the garage is closed. You may have some options, though. Your lease promises you a covered space, and the landlord has closed the garage with no reopening date. You can't safely hold back rent over this. You can send a written notice, and you may be able to claim damages for what the loss has cost you. A reduction by operation of law applies only if the closure was beyond the landlord's control, and the facts so far don't show that. What has the landlord said or done since you asked on April 15 about the repaving, and is work actually going on?

DETAILS

### Is the garage space something the landlord must provide?
Yes, as a lease promise. Lease §11 says: "Rent includes one reserved space in the covered, gated garage behind the building, space number 12." The lease has no clause letting the landlord close the garage or cut the rent while it is closed. It also doesn't say what happens to rent in that case. I don't know whether a local code covers this, because the codes aren't in this tool.

### Can you hold back rent?
I'd advise against it. The statute's rent-withholding defense (83.60(1)(b)) covers only a "material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)". That section lists building, housing and health codes, structural parts and plumbing. A parking space is a lease promise, not one of those items. If you stopped paying, you could face an eviction case without that defense. If you are sued, 83.60(2) has strict rules about paying rent into the court, but they wouldn't help you on this problem.

### Can you end the lease?
Possibly. Under 83.56(1), a tenant may end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with ... material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice". Four things must line up:
- **A lease promise failed.** The garage space is one.
- **"Material" is not settled.** One reading is that any failure of a lease promise counts. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted and how it affects your living there. You have had no covered parking for a while, but you do have street parking.
- **Written notice.** Your April 15 visit was verbal and doesn't count. The notice must name the problem and say you intend to end the lease because of it. Lease §7 says to hand it to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send it there by certified mail. Section 83.56(4) allows mailing or hand delivery. Lease §8 says there is no e-mail agreement. After delivery, the landlord has 7 days to fix the problem.
- **Rent already paid.** You paid May rent on May 1 knowing the garage was closed. Under 83.56(5)(a), paying rent with knowledge of a problem waives the right to end the lease "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." That is not settled here. One reading is that a garage that stays closed is a continuing problem, so you lost nothing. The other is that paying with knowledge gave up the right over this closure.

### Can you recover money?
Section 83.55 says an injured party "may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." It applies to lease promises and needs no special notice. Rent paid with knowledge may also affect the right to sue (83.56(5)(a)), with the same two readings as above. The winner in a suit may recover attorney fees and costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.

### Does the rent drop automatically?
Not as a general rule. Section 83.56(1)(b) reduces rent "in proportion to the loss of rental value" only when the failure is due to causes beyond the landlord's control and the landlord keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it. Here, the landlord ordered the repaving. Whether that was beyond its control, and whether it is working diligently, depends on facts we don't have. That is why I'm asking what the landlord has said or done. Even if this section applies, the statute says the lease is "terminated or altered by the parties". Whether that needs the landlord's agreement is unsettled. One reading is that both sides must agree. The other is that the reduction applies once the facts are met.

### Are you protected if you complain?
Section 83.64(1) bars a landlord from retaliating by raising rent, cutting services or bringing an eviction case "primarily because the landlord is retaliating." Its examples include a notice under 83.56(1). You must have acted in good faith, and a court decides what the landlord's motive was.

**Short answer:** You probably can't just stop paying rent. You also can't break the lease yet, but you can set up a lawful way to end it. Your lease promises working central air conditioning. Florida's repair law doesn't list air conditioning, so the rent-withholding defense probably doesn't cover it. (A local code might say otherwise. See below.) To end the lease, you must first deliver a written notice that says you will end it over the AC. Your June 4 portal request only asked for a repair, so it doesn't count as that notice. If you hand-deliver or certified-mail a proper notice and the AC isn't fixed 7 days after it arrives, you may end the lease. Don't pay rent in the meantime. Paying rent while you know about the problem can give up that right, and the law is unsettled on that.

The one thing I need to know is whether the office has given you any date for when the part will arrive, or said anything else about the repair.

DETAILS

### Can you stop paying rent?
- Holding back rent is a defense if your landlord sues to evict you. It applies only to a failure of the landlord's duties in section 83.51(1) (83.60(1)(b)). That subsection covers building, housing and health codes. If no code applies, it covers structural parts and plumbing. Air conditioning is in neither list.
- Your lease does promise it. Lease §11 says the landlord provides "refrigerator, stove, dishwasher, and central air conditioning" and "will keep them in working order." That is a lease duty, not an 83.51(1) duty, so the rent-withholding defense doesn't reach it.
- A local code might require air conditioning. I can't check that because local codes aren't in this tool. The city or county code office can tell you, and it can inspect. If a code does cover it, withholding rent could apply. You would still need a written notice saying you won't pay rent because of the problem. You would also need 7 days to pass after your landlord receives it (83.60(1)(b)).
- Withholding rent risks an eviction case. If you were sued, you would have to pay the rent into the court registry, or file a motion about the amount, within the time the summons states. If you miss that, you lose your defenses other than payment (83.60(2)).

### Can you end the lease?
Ending the lease can reach lease promises as well as 83.51(1) duties. The rule is in 83.56(1). It gives your landlord 7 days after delivery of your written notice to fix the problem. It requires "written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof." Here is where each condition stands:

1. **A duty your landlord failed.** The lease promises working AC (lease §11), and it has been out since June 3. Nothing you know of suggests you caused it, so the rule about tenant-caused damage doesn't apply (83.51(4)). Whether this failure is "material" is not settled. The statute doesn't define the word. One reading is that any failure of a promised item is material. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there. You have described 90-degree heat and about two weeks without a fix.
2. **A proper written notice.** Not met yet. Your portal request asked for the repair but didn't say you would end the lease. A portal message isn't a delivery method the statute names (83.56(4)). That subsection allows mailing, delivering a true copy, or e-mail under 83.505. Your lease says there is no e-mail agreement (lease §8). Lease §7 says to hand-deliver notices to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send them there by certified mail. Doing either meets the statute too.
3. **Seven days after delivery.** The 7 days count from the day the notice reaches the office. No notice has been delivered, so nothing is counting yet.
4. **No rent paid with knowledge of the problem.** Met so far. You paid June rent on June 1, before the AC failed, and you have paid nothing since. Rent due July 1 is the risk. If you pay rent knowing about the problem, you "waive" (give up) the right to end the lease over it, but "not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). Whether a still-unfixed AC counts as "continuing" is not settled. One reading says it does, so paying gives up nothing. The other says paying gives up the right to end the lease over this failure.

If all four conditions are met, you may end the lease (83.56(1)).

### Does the part on order change anything?
It might. If the delay is outside your landlord's control and your landlord keeps making every reasonable effort, a different rule applies (83.56(1)). It says the lease "may be terminated or altered by the parties." If the home is untenantable and you leave, you owe no rent for that time (83.56(1)(a)). If you stay, the rent is reduced in proportion to the lost rental value (83.56(1)(b)). The statute doesn't define "untenantable." It is also not settled whether this rule needs both sides to agree or applies automatically once its facts are met. Whether your landlord is really trying is why I'm asking about the part.

### Can you claim money for the broken AC?
Yes, possibly. Either side may recover damages caused by the other's failure to follow the lease or this law (83.55). The winner in a suit may also recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.

### Are you protected if you complain?
A landlord may not raise your rent, cut services, or file an eviction case primarily to retaliate against you for a good-faith complaint to a code office or a repair notice under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)). A court decides what the landlord's motive was.

**Short answer:** No to both, at least not yet. You can't safely stop paying rent. Your lease promises the air conditioning, and the law's rent-withholding defense doesn't cover a promise that comes only from the lease. You also can't end the lease yet, because your portal request asked for a repair but didn't say you would end the lease. You can end the lease if you send a proper written notice and the landlord still hasn't fixed the AC 7 days after it receives the notice. Whether this outage is serious enough to count is not settled. Have you handed the office anything on paper, or mailed it anything, about this?

DETAILS

### Is the AC your landlord's job to fix?
- Lease §11 says the landlord "will keep them in working order," and the list includes "central air conditioning." So the lease itself makes the AC the landlord's job.
- Florida's repair law, §83.51(1), lists codes, structure, and plumbing. §83.51(2)(a) adds pests, locks, common areas, garbage, and heat, running water and hot water. Neither list names air conditioning.
- So the AC is the landlord's duty because of the lease. It would also be a legal duty if a local building or housing code requires it. I can't check local codes. The Gainesville or Alachua County code office can tell you.
- Nothing you told me points to you causing the breakage, so §83.51(4) doesn't shift the blame to you.

### Can you stop paying rent?
- The rent-withholding defense in §83.60(1)(b) applies only to a "material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)." An AC promised only by the lease is not in that section, unless a local code covers it.
- If you stopped paying and the landlord sued to evict you, you likely couldn't use the broken AC as a defense. You would risk losing the apartment.
- Withholding would also need its own written notice saying you won't pay rent, then 7 days. Your portal request doesn't say that.
- If you were ever sued, §83.60(2) requires you to pay the rent into the court's registry or file a motion about it within a short time. The summons states the deadline. Missing it waives your defenses.

### Can you end the lease?
Under §83.56(1), a tenant may end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate." Here is where each condition stands:
1. **A promise the landlord failed to keep:** Met on the facts you gave. The lease promises working AC, and it has been out since June 3.
2. **Whether the failure is "material":** Not settled. The statute doesn't define the word. One reading is that any failure of a lease promise counts. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there. Your facts for the second reading are 90-degree heat and about two weeks without a fix.
3. **A proper written notice:** Not yet done. Your June 4 portal request didn't mention ending the lease. A portal message also isn't one of the delivery methods in §83.56(4), which are mailing, delivering a copy, or e-mail under §83.505. Your lease has no e-mail agreement. Lease §8 says "Landlord and Tenant have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail." Lease §7 says to hand-deliver to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send by certified mail. A notice should name the AC problem and say you will end the lease if it isn't fixed.
4. **7 days after delivery:** This hasn't started. The 7 days run from the day the notice reaches the landlord. I can count the date once you tell me when it was delivered.
5. **No rent paid with knowledge of the problem:** Met so far. You paid June rent on June 1, before the AC failed. July rent is due July 1. §83.56(5)(a) says paying rent with actual knowledge of a landlord's failure gives up the right to end the lease over that failure, "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." It is not settled whether an AC still broken after you pay counts as continuing. One reading is that it does, so paying gives up nothing. The other is that paying gives up ending the lease over this failure. So the timing of the notice and the July payment matters.

### Does the landlord's wait for a part change this?
- §83.56(1) has a separate path when a failure is "due to causes beyond the control of the landlord" and the landlord "has made and continues to make every reasonable effort" to fix it.
- In that case, if the home is "untenantable" and you leave, you owe no rent while it stays that way (§83.56(1)(a)). If you stay, rent is reduced in proportion to the lost rental value (§83.56(1)(b)).
- Whether a part on order meets that standard is open. It is also not settled whether "terminated or altered by the parties" means both sides must agree, or whether those results apply once the facts are met.
- The statute doesn't define "untenantable." The office said only that a part is on order and has said nothing since. That is a thin record of "every reasonable effort."

### Other options
- **Damages:** §83.55 lets you recover the damages caused by a landlord's failure to follow the lease. Paying rent with knowledge could affect this right too (§83.56(5)(a)). A suit can also make the loser pay the winner's attorney fees (§83.48).
- **Retaliation:** §83.64 bars a landlord from retaliating against you, for example by raising rent or filing to evict, because you sent a repair notice or complained to a code office. It protects good-faith actions, and a court decides the landlord's motive.

Your lease, section 11, says: "Rent includes one reserved space in the covered, gated garage behind the building, space number 12." That makes the space a lease promise. A local code might say something about it, but the codes are not stored in this tool, so I can't check. The lease has no clause letting the landlord close the garage. Section 11 is the only clause on parking.

### Can you hold back rent?
I advise against it. The rent-withholding defense in § 83.60(1)(b) covers only a "material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)". A lease-only promise like parking is outside it. If you stopped paying, the landlord could file an eviction case for non-payment, and you would likely have no defense to it.

### Does the rent go down automatically?
No, the law doesn't do it on its own, and the answer is open. Section 83.56(1)(b) lowers rent "in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." It applies only when the failure is "due to causes beyond the landlord's control" and the landlord keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it.
- **One reading:** the landlord ordered the repaving, so the cause was in its control, and this rule doesn't apply.
- **The other reading:** the work is a short-term project the landlord is pushing along, and the rule applies, so rent drops in proportion to the lost space.

What the landlord has told you about the work and its schedule would matter. So far, the office gave you no reopening date.

### Can you sue for money?

Maybe, but you haven't taken the first step.
